Titus Groan and Gormenghast by Mervyn Peake - my favorite novels, and the source of my username. They're actually the first two books in a trilogy, but the third doesn't do much for me.

The Book of the New Sun series by Gene Wolfe - tremendous novels - great story, great prose and so much more there than meets the eye, so they really reward re-reading.

Roadmarks by Roger Zelazny - I re-read a fair amount of Zelazny actually, but Roadmarks is my favorite and the one I re-read most regularly.

The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy series by Douglas Adams - they still make me laugh out loud.

Titus Groan and Gormenghast sound interesting. What genre are they in? I've only read The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy from your list, but Catch-22 is on my reading list.

They don't really fit in any genre.

They sort of superficially seem like fantasy, since the story all takes place in and around an enormous sprawling castle, but there are no fantasy elements to them - no magic or monsters or what-have-you. The story could have taken place in a village or town, but the castle gives it additional flavor, since it's a defined and self-contained space, with a clear demarcation between the inside and the outside. Plus it's just a wondrously bizarre place. Plus setting it in a castle ties in with the overarching theme of the books - (mostly unwelcome) change coming to a hidebound and tradition-obsessed society. Along with the castle there's, naturally, a ruling family, and they're the focal point of the obsession with tradition.

They're really just literature, with some fantastical elements. If I were to compare them with anything, it'd be 100 Years of Solitude by Gabriel Garcia Marquez. They're different in a lot of ways, but with the same basic outline - apparent allegories in an isolated and somewhat fantastical setting filled with vividly eccentric characters.

Parmesan and Garlic Crusted Potato Wedges. It's like the cheese that oozes out and gets all crispy on the pan... but on garlicky potatoes.

Those look tasty. Saving for later use. Recipe from img, in case that gets deleted sometime:

Here's the recipe! You can also view a really quick how-to video at https://youtu.be/gYw91rTOdPs if you'd like. Let me know if you have any questions! INGREDIENTS

4 russet potatoes, cut into wedges
4 cups water
1 tablespoon white or apple cider vinegar
1 tablespoon salt
1/4 cup butter, divided into tablespoon-sized pieces
4 ounces (about 1 cup) shredded parmesan cheese
4 large cloves garlic, minced
1/4 cup freshly chopped parsley
Zest of 1 lemon
Salt and pepper, to taste
Marinara or dip of choice, to serve

DIRECTIONS Place the potato wedges in a large pot, and add in the water, vinegar, and 1 tablespoon salt. Press down on the potatoes gently to make sure they're all submerged. Bring the pot to a gentle boil and continue to boil the potatoes for 10 minutes. Drain and pat the potatoes dry with paper towels. Set aside. Preheat oven to 400 degrees F. Set the butter on a large baking sheet. Transfer the baking sheet to the oven and allow the butter to melt as the oven preheats. Once the butter has fully melted, carefully remove the baking sheet from the oven. Sprinkle parmesan cheese evenly on top of the baking sheet. Do the same with the garlic. Place the potato wedges on top of the garlic and cheese layer, so that one of the skinless sides is touching the cheese. Bake for 45 minutes, or until the potatoes are lightly golden and the cheese has browned. As the potatoes cook, combine the parsley, lemon zest, salt and pepper in a small bowl and mix. Set aside. Let the potatoes sit for 5 minutes. This ensures that the cheese will stick to the potatoes instead of ripping off and staying on the pan. It's very important to leave them be so they can set. Using a metal spatula, break apart the cheese in-between each wedge and lift the baked cheese and wedges from the baking sheet. Plate and then sprinkle with the parsley mixture. Serve warm with marinara, ranch, or sauce of choice for dipping.

Socialism is a word that has meant many things to different people in different places at different times. The generally accepted definition is a system in which you don't have private ownership of the means of production, but rather the workers own the means of production (Sanders has rejected this publicly). This is different than Stalinism (which we uncritically call communism) which is a form of state-capitalism, where the state owns the means of production and plans the economy centrally (we'd need way better computers than we have to make an argument that this is feasible)--Sanders has rejected this publicly, too.

Sanders claims he's not a capitalist (he's certainly not doing capitalist things himself), but nothing he has proposed is really in conflict with the mixed economy we have, or the 20th century history of the country.
